## (a) One- and two-particle bases

Let f ∈ {n,p} denote neutron or proton, and s ∈ {↑,↓} denote spin. On a periodic cubic lattice with L³ sites, the dimensionless momenta are kᵢ = 2πnᵢ/L, with nᵢ integers modulo L. Define

 a†_{kfs} = L⁻³ᐟ² Σᵣ exp(i k·r) a†_{rfs},     |k,f,s⟩ = a†_{kfs}|0⟩.

These are a complete one-particle basis. For distinct one-particle orbitals, a spin-singlet pair is

 |f,g;k,q;S=0⟩ = [a†_{kf↑}a†_{qg↓} − a†_{kf↓}a†_{qg↑}]/√2 |0⟩.

For zero total momentum, q = −k. The neutron-neutron, proton-proton, and neutron-proton examples are

 |nn;k,S=0⟩ = [n†_{k↑}n†_{−k↓} − n†_{k↓}n†_{−k↑}]/√2 |0⟩,

 |pp;k,S=0⟩ = [p†_{k↑}p†_{−k↓} − p†_{k↓}p†_{−k↑}]/√2 |0⟩,

 |np;k,S=0⟩ = [n†_{k↑}p†_{−k↓} − n†_{k↓}p†_{−k↑}]/√2 |0⟩.

The np expression specifies a neutron at momentum k and a proton at −k; the exchanged momentum assignment is also possible. For two identical particles in the same zero-momentum orbital, the normalized nn state is n†_{0↑}n†_{0↓}|0⟩ (and likewise for pp); the generic expression with 1/√2 is not normalized in this coincident-orbital case. For identical particles, k and −k describe the same singlet state and should not be counted twice.

## (b) Matching the lattice kinetic scale

Fourier transforming the hopping term gives the free-particle dispersion

 ε_lat(k) = 2t Σᵢ[1 − cos(kᵢ)].

The zero-momentum mode has zero kinetic energy, so match the lowest nonzero lattice mode, k = (±2π/L,0,0) and permutations. Its energy is 2t[1 − cos(2π/L)]. In a periodic physical box, the lowest nonzero momentum has magnitude 2π/L_phy and nonrelativistic kinetic energy (2π/L_phy)²/(2M_phy), in natural units. Equating the two gives the exact finite-lattice result

 t = (2π/L_phy)² / {4M_phy[1 − cos(2π/L)]}.

For L ≫ 1, 1 − cos(2π/L) ≃ 2π²/L², so

 t ≃ L²/(2M_phy L_phy²) = 1/(2M_phy a²),     a = L_phy/L.

## (c) Lowest nonzero energy

Using ħc = 197.32698 MeV·fm, L_phy = 3.4 fm, and M_phy = 1634 MeV,

 E_min,nonzero = [2π(ħc)/L_phy]²/(2M_phy)
 = [2π(197.32698 MeV·fm)/(3.4 fm)]²/[2(1634 MeV)]
 ≃ 40.7 MeV.

This is kinetic energy above the rest mass; the zero-momentum mode has zero kinetic energy. The first momentum shell contains six momentum vectors (and twelve one-particle states when neutron spin is included).

## (d) Binding condition, coupling, and first excitation

For a zero-total-momentum pair, the free pair energy at relative lattice momentum k is 2ε_lat(k) = 4tΣᵢ[1 − cos(kᵢ)]. The on-site interaction has matrix element Ct/L³ between relative-momentum states. Consequently, a bound state at E = −B satisfies

 1/(Ct) = −(1/L³) Σ_k 1/{B + 4tΣᵢ[1 − cos(kᵢ)]}.

At infinite volume with fixed lattice spacing, this becomes

 1/C = −∫_[−π,π]³ d³q/(2π)³ · 1/{B/t + 4Σᵢ[1 − cos(qᵢ)]},

where q is dimensionless lattice momentum. This relation makes the missing input explicit: a numerical bare lattice C depends on t, and hence on the lattice spacing or ultraviolet cutoff. The binding energy B = 17.8 MeV alone does not determine a unique numerical C. Taking L → ∞ at fixed spacing retains the lattice cutoff; taking a → 0 is a different limit and requires a renormalization prescription.

The binding energy does fix a physical scale in the zero-range continuum approximation. For two equal masses, the relative kinetic energy is k²/M, so

 κ = √(MB) = √[(1634 MeV)(17.8 MeV)] ≃ 170.5 MeV ≃ 0.864 fm⁻¹,
 a_s = 1/κ ≃ 1.16 fm,

where a_s is the zero-range scattering length if effective-range effects are neglected. These physical quantities do not specify the regulator-dependent lattice C.

In infinite volume, the unbound relative spectrum is E_rel = k²/M ≥ 0. Its continuum threshold is E = 0, which is 17.8 MeV above the bound state at −17.8 MeV. This threshold is not a discrete, normalizable first excited state; there is no discrete first excited level in the stated limit.

## (e) Second excited state and degeneracy

In the infinite-volume limit there is no discrete second excited state or finite degeneracy for such a level: the scattering spectrum is a continuum for E ≥ 0. A finite box would discretize that spectrum, but the interacting excited energies and degeneracies would depend on the box size and regulator, which are not specified. If “first excitation” is intended to mean the continuum threshold, it is at E = 0 relative to the two-particle free threshold, or 17.8 MeV above the bound-state ground energy; it is still not a discrete excited level.
